The theory of '''accessible categories''' is a part of [[mathematics]], specifically of [[category theory]]. It attempts to describe categories in terms of the "size" (a [[cardinal number]]) of the operations needed to generate their objects.

The theory originates in the work of [[Alexander Grothendieck|Grothendieck]] completed by 1969,<ref>
{{Citation
  | last = Grothendieck   | first = Alexander   
  | title = Théorie des Topos et Cohomologie Étale des Schémas 
  | publisher = Springer
  | series = Lecture Notes in Mathematics 269
  | year = 1972|display-authors=etal}}
</ref> and Gabriel and Ulmer (1971).<ref>
{{Citation
  | last = Gabriel   | first = P   
  | last2 = Ulmer    | first2 = F
  | title = Lokal Präsentierbare Kategorien 
  | publisher = Springer
  | series = Lecture Notes in Mathematics 221
  | year = 1971}}
</ref> It has been further developed in 1989 by [[Michael Makkai]] and Robert Paré, with motivation coming from [[model theory]], a branch of [[mathematical logic]].<ref>
{{Citation
  | last = Makkai   | first = Michael   
  | last2 = Paré    | first2 = Robert
  | title = Accessible categories: The foundation of Categorical Model Theory 
  | publisher = AMS
  | series = Contemporary Mathematics
  | year = 1989
  | isbn =  0-8218-5111-X }}
</ref>
A standard text book by Adámek and Rosický appeared in 1994.<ref name=""AdámekRosický"">{{cite book | last=Adámek   | first=Jiří | last2=Rosický  | first2=Jiří | title=Locally Presentable and Accessible Categories | publisher=Cambridge University Press | date=10 March 1994 | isbn=978-0-521-42261-1 | doi=10.1017/cbo9780511600579 }}</ref>
Accessible categories also have applications in [[homotopy theory]].<ref name="ref1">J. Rosický [https://arxiv.org/abs/0708.2185 "On combinatorial model categories"], ''[[arXiv]]'', 16 August 2007. Retrieved on 19 January 2008.</ref><ref name="ref3">Rosický, J. "Injectivity and accessible categories." ''Cubo Matem. Educ'' 4 (2002): 201-211.</ref> Grothendieck continued the development of the theory for homotopy-theoretic purposes in his (still partly unpublished) 1991 manuscript ''Les dérivateurs''.<ref>
{{Citation
  | last = Grothendieck   | first = Alexander   
  | title = Les dérivateurs 
  | publisher = manuscript
  | series = Contemporary Mathematics
  | year = 1991}} ([https://web.archive.org/web/20071024032414/http://www.institut.math.jussieu.fr/~maltsin/groth/Derivateurs.html Les Dérivateurs: Texte d'Alexandre Grothendieck.  Édité par M. Künzer, J. Malgoire, G. Maltsiniotis])
</ref>
Some properties of accessible categories depend on the [[Axiomatic set theory|set universe]] in use, particularly on the [[cardinal number|cardinal]] properties and [[Vopěnka's principle]].<ref name="ref2">Adamek/Rosický 1994, chapter 6</ref>

=={{mvar|&kappa;}}-directed colimits and {{mvar|&kappa;}}-presentable objects==
Let <math>\kappa</math> be an infinite [[regular cardinal]], i.e. a [[cardinal number]] that is not the sum of a smaller number of smaller cardinals; examples are <math>\aleph _{0}</math> ([[Aleph number|aleph-0]]), the first infinite cardinal number, and <math>\aleph_{1} </math>, the first uncountable cardinal). A [[partially ordered set]] <math>(I, \leq) </math> is called '''<math>\kappa</math>-directed''' if every subset <math>J </math> of <math>I </math> of cardinality less than <math>\kappa</math> has an upper bound in <math>I </math>. In particular, the ordinary [[directed set]]s are precisely the <math>\aleph_0</math>-directed sets.

Now let <math>C</math> be a [[category (mathematics)|category]]. A [[direct limit]] (also known as a directed colimit) over a <math>\kappa</math>-directed set <math>(I, \leq) </math> is called a '''<math>\kappa</math>-directed colimit'''. An object <math>X</math> of <math>C</math> is called <math>\kappa</math>'''-presentable''' if the [[Hom functor]] <math>\operatorname{Hom}(X,-)</math> preserves all <math>\kappa</math>-directed colimits in <math>C</math>. It is clear that every <math>\kappa</math>-presentable object is also <math>\kappa'</math>-presentable whenever  <math>\kappa\leq\kappa'</math>, since every <math>\kappa'</math>-directed colimit is also a <math>\kappa</math>-directed colimit in that case. A <math>\aleph_0</math>-presentable object is called '''finitely presentable'''.

===Examples===
*In the category '''[[Category of sets|Set]]''' of all sets, the finitely presentable objects coincide with the finite sets. The <math>\kappa</math>-presentable objects are the sets of cardinality smaller than <math>\kappa</math>.
*In the [[Category of groups|category of all groups]], an object is finitely presentable if and only if it is a [[Presentation of a group#finitely presented|finitely presented group]], i.e. if it has a presentation with finitely many generators and finitely many relations. For uncountable regular <math>\kappa</math>, the <math>\kappa</math>-presentable objects are precisely the groups with cardinality smaller than <math>\kappa</math>.
*In the [[Category of modules|category of left <math>R</math>-modules]] over some (unitary, associative) [[Ring (mathematics)|ring]] <math>R</math>, the finitely presentable objects are precisely the [[Finitely generated module#Finitely presented, finitely related, and coherent modules|finitely presented module]]s.

==<span class="anchor" id="locally_presentable"></span> {{mvar|&kappa;}}-accessible and locally presentable categories==
The category <math>C</math> is called '''<math>\kappa</math>-accessible''' provided that:

* <math>C</math> has all <math>\kappa</math>-directed colimits
* <math>C</math> contains a set <math>P</math> of <math>\kappa</math>-presentable objects such that every object of <math>C</math> is a <math>\kappa</math>-directed colimit of objects of <math>P</math>.

An <math>\aleph_0</math>-accessible category is called '''finitely accessible'''.
A category is called '''accessible''' if it is <math>\kappa</math>-accessible for some infinite regular cardinal <math>\kappa</math>. 
When an accessible category is also [[cocomplete]], it is called '''locally presentable'''.

A functor <math>F : C \to D</math> between <math>\kappa</math>-accessible categories is called '''<math>\kappa</math>-accessible''' provided that <math>F</math> preserves <math>\kappa</math>-directed colimits.

===Examples===

* The category '''Set''' of all sets and functions is locally finitely presentable, since every set is the direct limit of its finite subsets, and finite sets are finitely presentable.
* The category <math>R</math>-Mod of (left) <math>R</math>-modules is locally finitely presentable for any ring <math>R</math>.
* The category of [[simplicial set]]s is finitely accessible.
* The category Mod(T) of models of some [[first-order theory]] T with countable signature is <math>\aleph_1</math> -accessible. <math>\aleph_1</math> -presentable objects are models with a countable number of elements.
* Further examples of locally presentable categories are finitary algebraic categories (i.e. the categories corresponding to [[Variety (universal algebra)|varieties of algebras]] in [[universal algebra]]) and [[Grothendieck category|Grothendieck categories]].

==Theorems==
One can show that every locally presentable category is also [[Complete category|complete]].<ref>Adamek/Rosický 1994, remark 1.56</ref> Furthermore, a category is locally presentable if and only if it is equivalent to the category of models of a limit [[Sketch (mathematics)|sketch]].<ref>Adamek/Rosický 1994, corollary 1.52</ref>

[[Adjoint functors]] between locally presentable categories have a particularly simple characterization. A functor <math>F : C \to D</math> between locally presentable categories:

* is a left adjoint if and only if it preserves small colimits,
* is a right adjoint if and only if it preserves small limits and is accessible.
